summary: Defines the EAP early authentication problem, where a mobile device uses EAP to set up keying material on a target attachment point before it arrives. The document discusses the problem in detail. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When a phone moves from one base station to another, the call can be interrupted while the new network checks who the user is. This RFC describes the problem of doing that check before the phone even arrives, and the three ways the signalling could be arranged.

questions: what is the eap early auth problem
subtitle: The problem of authenticating a phone at the network it is about to join, before it gets there.

tldr.problem: When a mobile device moves to a new access network, the handover is held up by a full EAP exchange with the new network, and that delay is more than a real-time call can tolerate.
tldr.mechanism: EAP early authentication means the device authenticates to the candidate attachment point over the network it is already using, so the keys are ready before it moves.
tldr.outcome: It is a problem statement, not a solution. It describes three usage models, two architectural problems that still need solving, and a list of gaps in the AAA protocols.

facts.label: Early authentication session lifetime
facts.value: Typically valid only for a short time

today: RFC 5836 is an Informational document published in April 2010, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a problem statement rather than a specification: it describes the early authentication problem, the models for analysing it, the architectural questions still open, and the gaps in the AAA protocols that would have to be filled.

sections.title: The Problem and the Vocabulary
sections.content:
When a mobile device moves from one access network to another during an active session and changes its attachment point, the session may be disrupted by the delay the handover causes. What counts as acceptable depends on the application. For voice over IP, ITU-T G.114 recommends a steady-state end-to-end delay of 150 ms as the upper limit and rates 400 ms as generally unacceptable. A streaming application has tolerable packet-error rates ranging from 0.1 to 0.00001 with a transfer delay of less than 300 ms. The stated ultimate objective is seamless handover with low latency, even when the handover is between different link technologies or between different AAA realms.

The delay comes from two places: the rebinding of the device's association at several layers of the protocol stack, and the additional round trips needed for a new EAP exchange. Delays inside each protocol layer affect the ongoing multimedia application and the data traffic in the client. A handover also usually requires authentication and authorisation to acquire or modify resources, and in most cases these need a central authority in a realm, which may be far away. That delay adds to the handover latency and so affects the running application. This document focuses on reducing the delay caused by EAP authentication.

The terminology section defines the parts. An attachment point is a device, such as a wireless access point, that acts as a gateway between access clients and a network; in this document it must also support EAP authenticator functionality and may act as an AAA client. The authenticator is the end of the link that initiates EAP authentication, and the peer is the entity that responds to it and requires authentication. An EAP server terminates the EAP authentication method with the peer; EAP servers are often, but not necessarily, co-located with AAA servers, using an AAA protocol to talk to remote pass-through authenticators. The AAA realm is the set of access networks within the scope of a specific AAA server, so a device moving between attachment points in the same realm is still served by the same AAA server. The Master Session Key is keying material derived between the EAP peer and server and exported by the EAP method.
sections.plainLanguage: Moving between networks costs time, and a call cannot afford much of it. This RFC sets out the terms it uses for the pieces involved: the phone, the point it is plugged into now, the point it might move to, and the server that checks the user's account.

sections.title: Two Ways to Solve It
sections.content:
Handover has two steps: preparation, which discovers candidate attachment points and selects a target from them, and execution, which sets up the layer 2 and layer 3 connectivity with that target. Preparation is outside the scope of this document. Execution currently includes network access authentication and authorisation performed directly with the target network, which may include a full EAP authentication when there is no particular optimisation for handover key management. After a successful EAP authentication, a secure association procedure is typically performed between the device and the target to derive new link-layer encryption keys from the EAP keying material such as the MSK. The handover latency introduced by a full EAP authentication has proved higher than real-time applications can accept, so reducing it is a necessary objective.

Two existing specifications are cited as examples. In IEEE 802.11 wireless networks, access authentication and authorisation means a new IEEE 802.1X message exchange with the authenticator in the target attachment point, which runs an EAP exchange with the authentication server. There has been optimisation work in the IEEE, but it has been scoped to IEEE link-layer technologies: the work of the IEEE 802.11f and 802.11r Task Groups applies only to intra-technology handovers. In 3GPP Technical Specification 33.402, network access authentication and authorisation happens after the layer 2 connection is established between the device and a non-3GPP target access network, and involves an EAP exchange between the device and the 3GPP AAA server via that target access network. Those procedures are not really independent of link technology, because they assume either that the authenticator lies in the evolved packet system network, or that separate authentications are performed in the access network and then in that network.

Optimised solutions for secure inter-authenticator handovers fall into two families. Security context transfer moves reusable key context to the target attachment point, and comes in horizontal and vertical forms. Horizontal transfer, from the serving point to the target, is not recommended, because compromising one attachment point might lead to compromising another, the so-called domino effect. Vertical transfer is like the initial establishment of keying material: the keys are sent from a trusted server to the target as a direct result of a successful authentication. ERP specifies vertical context transfer using existing EAP keying material obtained from the home AAA server during the initial authentication, deriving a cryptographically independent re-authentication key and transmitting it to the target after a successful ERP authentication. This reduces handover delay for intra-realm handovers by removing the need to run full EAP authentication with the home EAP server. In the case of an inter-realm handover, however, either ERP does not apply or an extra optimisation mechanism is needed to establish a key on the target.

EAP early authentication performs the AAA-based authentication and authorisation for a candidate attachment point while the ongoing data communication is still running over the serving access network, with the goal of completing the AAA signalling before the device moves. Its applicability is limited to scenarios where candidate authenticators can be discovered and movement can be predicted accurately. Its effectiveness may also be less significant for inter-technology handovers where using several technologies at once is not a major concern.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two answers. One is to carry the keys over from the old network to the new one. The other is to authenticate against the new network in advance, over the connection the device already has.

sections.title: How the Handovers Differ
sections.content:
The complexity of the authentication and authorisation part of a handover depends on whether the EAP server changes. Taking the case where the authenticators operate in pass-through mode, so that the EAP server is co-located with an AAA server, the RFC gives a strict hierarchy.

First comes the inter-attachment-point handover with a common AAA server, where the target and serving attachment points are different entities but the AAA server is the same. There are two sub-cases: the AAA server is common because both attachment points lie within the same network, or the AAA server is common because the AAA entities in the serving and candidate networks proxy to an AAA server in the home realm. Second comes the inter-AAA-realm handover, where the target and serving points are different entities and the AAA servers also differ, so authentication in the candidate network needs a second set of user credentials.

A third case exists where one or both authenticators are co-located with an EAP server. This has some of the characteristics of an inter-AAA-realm handover, but offers less flexibility for resolving the early authentication problem.

Orthogonally to that, one can distinguish an intra-technology handover from an inter-technology handover, thinking of the link technologies involved. In the inter-technology case it is highly probable that the authenticators will differ, and the most likely cases are the second sub-case of the common-AAA-server handover, or the inter-AAA-realm handover.
sections.plainLanguage: The harder the handover, the more the setup changes. Moving between two base stations that share one account server is easy. Moving to a network run by a different organisation means a second set of credentials.

sections.title: Three Models for the Signalling
sections.content:
There are cases where early authentication applies but ERP does not work, so the RFC builds three usage models to analyse the problem against. They differ by who talks to whom: the serving attachment point is not involved in early authentication at all, it interacts only with the candidate attachment point, or it interacts with the AAA server. The models assume the candidate and serving attachment points are different entities, and that there is no direct layer 2 connectivity between the peer and the candidate attachment point.

The direct pre-authentication model. The serving point is not involved in the EAP exchange and only forwards the early authentication traffic as it would any other data. The model assumes the device can discover the candidate authenticators and establish direct IP communication with them, and it applies to any of the cases in the classification above. In the signalling, EAP runs over the MD-CAP signalling at layer 3 between the device and the candidate authenticator, and over AAA between the candidate authenticator and the EAP server.

The indirect pre-authentication model. Here a trust relationship is assumed between the serving network or realm and the candidate network or realm, and the serving point is involved in the early authentication signalling. The model is needed if the peer cannot discover the identity of the candidate authenticators, or if direct IP communication between the device and the candidate is not possible because of security or network topology. The role of the serving point is to forward the early authentication signalling between the device and the candidate; the role of the candidate is to forward the early authentication signalling between the peer, via the serving point, and the EAP server, and to receive the transported keying material. The signalling path then has two segments: peer-to-serving-point over layer 2 or layer 3, and serving-point-to-candidate over layer 3.

The authenticated anticipatory keying model. Here it is assumed there is no trust relationship between the serving and candidate points, so the serving point must interact with the AAA server directly. The serving point communicates with the peer on one side and exchanges authenticated anticipatory keying signalling with the EAP server on the other. The role of the candidate authenticator is to receive the transported keying material from the EAP server and to act as the serving attachment point once the handover happens. The device-to-serving-point signalling is over layer 2 or layer 3; the serving-point-to-AAA and AAA-to-candidate segments operate over layer 3.
sections.plainLanguage: Three shapes are possible. The phone can talk to the new base station directly, the old base station can relay for it, or the old base station can ask the account server to pass the keys across directly.

sections.title: Discovery, Context Binding and AAA Gaps
sections.content:
Two architectural issues are named. Authenticator discovery. Early authentication requires the identity of a candidate attachment point to be discovered by the peer, by a serving attachment point, or by some other entity before the handover. An attachment point discovery protocol is typically defined as a separate protocol from the early authentication protocol; the IEEE 802.21 Information Service, for example, provides a link-layer-independent mechanism for obtaining information about neighbouring networks by defining a set of Information Elements, one of which holds the IP address of an attachment point, and queries for that element can be used for authenticator discovery. If such a mechanism is used, discovery needs a database of information about the target network, and provisioning a server with that database is another issue in itself.

Context binding. When a candidate authenticator uses different EAP transport protocols for normal and early authentication, a mechanism is needed to bind the link-layer-independent context carried over the early authentication signalling to the link-layer-specific context of the link that is about to be established. The link-layer-independent context includes the identities of the peer and authenticator and the MSK; the link-layer-specific context includes the link-layer addresses of the peer and the candidate authenticator. Binding can happen before or after the peer changes its point of attachment. Two approaches are given: communicating the link-layer context as opaque data over the early authentication signalling, or running EAP over the candidate's link layer after the peer arrives, using short-term credentials generated by the early authentication and shared between the peer and the candidate authenticator. In both approaches the binding has to be made securely, and the peer is not fully authorised by the candidate authenticator until it completes the link-layer secure association procedure.

Several AAA issues follow. Most AAA documents do not distinguish a normal authentication from an early one. Users who may not have more than one logon session at a time cannot perform early authentication while already in a session, and the AAA server has no way of telling the two requests apart. Session lifetime attributes exist for normal sessions, but an early authenticated session is typically valid only for a short time because the peer has not finished authenticating at the target link layer, and there is no way for the AAA server to tell the client or the peer when it will expire. If the peer has not yet moved and sees the session expiring, it may authenticate again, so a limiting mechanism is needed to avoid unlimited attempts. Once the peer has attached, it must convert its state from early authenticated to fully attached and authorised, and if the AAA server needs to tell the two apart the protocol may need a mechanism for that, which matters for billing when the policy does not charge for a peer until it is fully attached. Where the peer cycles between a network it has fully authenticated to and another one, it should be possible to convert the fully authenticated state into an early authenticated one, which raises the problems of session lifetime and keying material caching. Where the peer must choose between several candidates, authenticating with several of them amplifies the authorisation problem. An inter-AAA-realm handover requires the early authentication to be performed through the visited realm with the home realm's AAA server, and the visited realm's AAA needs the home realm's identity information to route the traffic, with both the peer and the AAA needing realm identities to generate the key for mutual authentication. Finally, the existing specifications mostly deal with homogeneous 802.11 networks: AAA attributes such as Calling-Station-ID may need to cover other access technologies, and an inter-technology handover may require a change of the peer identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things have to be worked out: how the phone finds out about the network it is moving to, and how the keys it got early are tied to the new radio link. The account protocols also need changing, because they cannot tell an early login from a normal one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The section covers the threats that early authentication introduces to the EAP model. General issues with EAP and handover are described in other documents.

Because early authentication has to work across multiple attachment points, any solution has to consider two threats. First, a resource consumption denial-of-service attack is possible, where an attacker that is not on the same IP link as the legitimate peer or the candidate authenticator may send unprotected early authentication messages to the legitimate peer or the candidate authenticator, which then spends computational and bandwidth resources on processing them. This attack is possible in both the direct and the indirect pre-authentication scenarios. To mitigate it, the candidate network or authenticator may apply non-cryptographic packet filtering so that only early authentication messages from a specific set of serving networks or authenticators are processed. On the peer side, a simple solution is to let the peer always initiate EAP early authentication and never accept initiation from an authenticator.

Second, the channel binding problem described in RFC 5247 has to be considered, because a lack of channel binding may enable an authenticator to impersonate another authenticator or to communicate incorrect information out of band, for example over a AAA or lower-layer protocol. The RFC notes that such an impersonation attack is relatively easier to launch against early authentication than against normal authentication, because an attacker does not need to be physically on the same link as the legitimate peer in order to send an early authentication trigger to the peer.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the early messages travel across the network, anyone can send them. The document suggests filtering by source and, on the phone's side, only ever starting the exchange itself.

viz.caption: THE AAA ISSUES THE RFC LISTS

items.title: Authorisation
items.text: A user with one session already open may not be allowed to authenticate again early.

items.title: Lifetime
items.text: Nobody can tell the peer when the early session will expire.

items.title: Retries
items.text: A peer that has not moved yet may authenticate again and again, so a limit is needed.

items.title: Completion of attachment
items.text: The protocol may need to say whether the peer is early authenticated or fully attached, for billing.

items.title: Session resumption
items.text: Converting a fully authenticated state back into an early one raises caching problems.

items.title: Multiple candidates
items.text: Authenticating with several candidates at once multiplies the authorisation problem.

items.title: Inter-realm handover
items.text: The visited realm needs the home realm's identity to route the traffic and to make the key.

items.title: Inter-technology support
items.text: Most of the existing work assumes 802.11, and the peer identifier may have to change.
